EIML 1 · EurIPS 2025

Epistemic Intelligence in Machine Learning

This page preserves the published record of EIML 1 · EurIPS 2025. Dates, affiliations, and submission information refer to that edition.

About this edition

Reliable decisions require AI systems to acknowledge gaps in their knowledge, especially when data or assumptions change. The first EIML workshop focused on this epistemic uncertainty—the uncertainty arising from a learner's limited knowledge—and its implications for prediction, learning, and decision-making.

The programme connected machine learning, statistics, decision theory, and philosophy. It examined how uncertainty should be represented and evaluated, how learning can remain reliable under incomplete information, and how principled uncertainty models can scale to modern AI systems.

Topics

Representing and measuring uncertainty
  • Foundations for describing limited knowledge, including Bayesian methods, imprecise probabilities, fuzzy logic, belief functions, and possibility theory.
  • Properties and comparisons of uncertainty representations, evaluation criteria, and benchmarks.
  • Distinguishing uncertainty due to limited knowledge from randomness inherent in the data.
Prediction with incomplete knowledge
  • Predictive models that express uncertainty, including Bayesian, evidential, and credal approaches.
  • Reliable generalisation when training and test distributions differ, with domain adaptation and robustness analysis.
  • Detecting unfamiliar inputs, handling incorrect model assumptions, and learning from partial or vague supervision.
Decisions and learning under uncertainty
  • Decisions that account for risk and ambiguity, and uncertainty in generative models.
  • Choosing informative data or experiments through active learning, Bayesian experimental design, and uncertainty-aware optimisation.
  • Reinforcement, continual, and online learning; scalable uncertainty methods for transformers, diffusion models, and other large architectures.

Panel discussion

Is Probability Sufficient for Next Generation Epistemic AI?

The panel considered which representations of uncertainty intelligent systems need, bringing together theoretical, practical, and philosophical perspectives on probability and alternative frameworks.

Call for papers

Submission information from the original call, retained for reference.

The workshop used OpenReview with anonymised submissions and double-blind review. The call specified 4–6 pages, excluding references and supplementary material, using the EurIPS 2025 style files linked below.

Original, unpublished research and work under review elsewhere were eligible; prior non-archival dissemination was also allowed. EIML was a non-archival workshop, with authors responsible for checking other venues' policies.

Attendance was primarily in person, with poster presentations encouraged. The call advertised selected 10-minute spotlights; the final programme allocated each oral presentation 12 minutes plus 3 minutes for questions.

All authors needed OpenReview profiles. The stated language-model policy permitted their use only for general writing assistance.
